title: Alcohols, ethers and epoxides
note: Alcohol oxidation depends on class: 1° gives an aldehyde (PCC) or a carboxylic acid (Jones), 2° gives a ketone, and 3° resists oxidation. OH is a poor leaving group until it is protonated or converted to a tosylate or halide. Epoxides open at the less hindered carbon under basic conditions and at the more substituted carbon under acidic conditions.

read.title: Turning OH into something useful
text: Alcohols are among the most versatile starting materials, but the hydroxyl group itself is a poor leaving group because hydroxide is a strong base. Chemists convert it into something better. Strong acid protonates it to water, which leaves easily: tertiary alcohols then react with HBr by SN1, and heating with sulfuric acid gives alkenes by E1. For primary and secondary alcohols, PBr₃ or SOCl₂ makes the alkyl halide without carbocations, and tosyl chloride makes a tosylate, a leaving group as good as a halide.

Oxidation depends on how many hydrogens sit on the carbinol carbon. A primary alcohol can lose two of them: PCC or Dess–Martin periodinane stops at the aldehyde, while chromic acid in water continues to the carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone. A tertiary alcohol has no such hydrogen and is not oxidized.

Ethers are usually unreactive, which makes them good solvents, but strong HBr or HI cleaves them. Epoxides are different: ring strain makes them reactive. A strong nucleophile under basic conditions attacks the less hindered carbon by SN2. In acid, the protonated epoxide opens at the more substituted carbon, which carries more of the positive charge.

q.q: Why is a tertiary alcohol not oxidized by chromic acid?
o: Its carbinol carbon has no hydrogen
